prompt: How do JPA and Hibernate relate to each other?
hint: One of them is only a set of interfaces and annotations.

choices.text: Hibernate is a specification, and JPA is Spring's implementation of it
choices.why: The other way round, and Spring is not part of it: JPA is the specification, Hibernate implements it, and Spring Boot only configures it.

choices.text: JPA is a specification, and Hibernate is one implementation of it
choices.why: Right. `jakarta.persistence` defines the annotations, the `EntityManager` and JPQL; Hibernate does the work. EclipseLink implements the same specification.

choices.text: They are two competing mappers, and a project picks one or the other
choices.why: A project picks an implementation of JPA, and Hibernate is one. Code written against `jakarta.persistence` runs on Hibernate without naming it.

choices.text: JPA is the older name of Hibernate, kept for compatibility
choices.why: The old name is of the specification itself: Java Persistence API, now Jakarta Persistence. Hibernate has always been a separate project.

prompt: A colleague says that with Hibernate the application stops sending SQL to the database and works on objects kept in memory instead. What is wrong with that?
hint: Where does every entity come from, and how does a change get stored?

choices.text: Nothing: Hibernate keeps the entities cached in memory and reads the database only once, at start-up
choices.why: This is the wrong picture the lesson starts from. Every entity is loaded by a `SELECT` when it is asked for, and the catalogue report's log shows one.

choices.text: Every entity still comes from a SELECT and every change leaves as an UPDATE; Hibernate writes them
choices.why: Right. What changes is who writes the statements and when they run. The SQL log in this lesson shows each one.

choices.text: Hibernate sends JPQL to the database instead of SQL
choices.why: The database never sees JPQL. Hibernate translates `select b from Book b` into SQL for PostgreSQL before sending it.

choices.text: Hibernate only sends SQL when save() is called
choices.why: The reprice demonstration changed a price with no save at all, and an `UPDATE` went out at the commit. Loading sends SQL too.

prompt: Match each thing in the Java code to what stands for it in PostgreSQL.
hint: Class to table, object to row, and the reference to the column that replaces it.

pairs.left: the field author, holding an Author
pairs.right: the column author_id, holding a number

prompt: Why does this lesson drop and recreate the bookshop database instead of letting the new schema.sql run against it?
hint: Read the first words of each statement in schema.sql.

choices.text: Hibernate refuses to start when a database already contains tables
choices.why: With `ddl-auto=none` Hibernate does not touch tables at all, and it starts against existing ones every day. The failure comes from `data.sql`.

choices.text: PostgreSQL cannot add a foreign key to a table that already has rows
choices.why: It can, with `ALTER TABLE`, as long as every row satisfies it. Nothing here runs an `ALTER`; the old table is simply left as it was.

choices.text: The role bookshop loses its password when the schema changes
choices.why: The role and its password belong to the cluster, not to a schema, and the two commands keep the same owner.

choices.text: `IF NOT EXISTS` keeps lesson 9's `book` table as it was
choices.why: Right. The old table exists, so the statement does nothing, and the `INSERT` naming `author_id` meets a table without it. The failure is shown in the section on the entity manager.

prompt: What does `spring.jpa.hibernate.ddl-auto=none` tell Hibernate?
hint: DDL is CREATE, ALTER and DROP.

choices.text: To leave the tables alone: they are created by something else
choices.why: Right. Here `schema.sql` owns them, and lesson 13 hands them to a migration tool.

choices.text: To create the tables from the entities when the application starts
choices.why: That is `create`. It is tempting on the first day, and then the schema is whatever the Java says that morning.

choices.text: To check that the tables match the entities, and refuse to start if not
choices.why: That is `validate`, which lesson 13 switches on.

choices.text: To run no SQL at all until the first request arrives
choices.why: `ddl-auto` is about the schema only. The catalogue report runs a `SELECT` at start-up whatever this says.

prompt: What does `spring-boot-starter-data-jpa` bring into the bookshop? Choose all that apply.
hint: The section ran `mvn dependency:tree` and kept six lines.

choices.text: Hibernate itself, `hibernate-core`
choices.why: Right: the implementation of the specification.

choices.text: The JPA annotations and interfaces, `jakarta.persistence-api`
choices.why: Right: what the entities and repositories import.

choices.text: Everything the JDBC starter brought, HikariCP included
choices.why: Right. It depends on `spring-boot-starter-jdbc`, which is why replacing one with the other loses nothing.

choices.text: The PostgreSQL driver
choices.why: The driver is still its own dependency in the pom, with `runtime` scope. The starter works with any database whose driver you add.

choices.text: A migration tool for the schema
choices.why: No starter in this pom manages migrations. Lesson 13 adds Flyway for that.

prompt: Lesson 5's `Book` was a record. Why is it a class with a `protected` constructor now?
hint: Think of how Hibernate builds the object, and of what happens to it afterwards.

choices.text: A record cannot hold a reference to another record, so a book could not point at its author
choices.why: It can; lesson 5's `Book` could have held an `Author` record. The problem is how the mapper creates and changes its objects.

choices.text: Hibernate creates it empty, fills it in and later spots changes, and a record allows none of that
choices.why: Right. The `protected` no-argument constructor is for Hibernate; application code uses the one that takes every value.

choices.text: Spring cannot inject a record into a service
choices.why: Entities are not injected at all. Spring injects the repository; Hibernate creates the entities.

choices.text: Jackson cannot turn a record into JSON
choices.why: Jackson turns records into JSON happily: `BookResponse` is a record, and it is what the API sends.

prompt: With `@ManyToOne(fetch = FetchType.LAZY)`, what does a freshly loaded `Book` hold in its `author` field?
hint: It knows the author's id and nothing else.

choices.text: `null`, until the code calls a setter
choices.why: The field is never `null` for a book with an author; and the entity has no setter for it.

choices.text: The author itself, read from the same SELECT that loaded the book a moment earlier
choices.why: That is what `join fetch` asks for. On its own, `LAZY` leaves the author out of the book's query.

choices.text: The number from the `author_id` column, stored as a `Long` until somebody needs the name
choices.why: The field's type is `Author`. The number is inside the proxy, which is an `Author` subclass Hibernate generated.

choices.text: A proxy that loads the author's row the first time its data is asked for
choices.why: Right. The `getName()` in `BookResponse.from` is what sends the second statement in the section on the entity manager.

prompt: Somebody removes `fetch = FetchType.LAZY` and leaves `@ManyToOne(optional = false)`. What fetch type does the relationship have then?
hint: JPA's default for a single reference is the opposite of what this lesson recommends.

choices.text: LAZY, because Hibernate makes every relationship lazy
choices.why: Hibernate follows the specification's defaults, and for `@ManyToOne` that is `EAGER`.

choices.text: LAZY, because `optional = false` implies it
choices.why: `optional = false` says every book has an author, which lets Hibernate join with `inner join`. It says nothing about when the author is loaded.

choices.text: EAGER, the specification's default for `@ManyToOne`
choices.why: Right, which is why the bookshop writes `LAZY` out. The section on N+1 shows that `EAGER` does not prevent the extra queries anyway.

choices.text: None: the annotation refuses to compile without a fetch type
choices.why: `fetch` has a default, so the annotation is complete without it. That default is the trap.

prompt: The id column is a `bigserial`, so the database invents each number. The entity says so with `@GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.___)`.
In the JPQL query `select b from Book b order by b.id`, what is `Book`?
hint: JPQL never names a table.

choices.text: The name of the table in PostgreSQL
choices.why: The table happens to be called `book`, but JPQL names the entity. Rename the class and the query changes; rename the table and only the mapping does.

choices.text: The entity class `Book`
choices.why: Right. JPQL speaks of entities and fields, and Hibernate writes the SQL with the table and column names.

choices.text: A view Hibernate creates in the database at start-up
choices.why: Hibernate creates nothing here (`ddl-auto=none`), and the SQL it sends reads the `book` table directly.

choices.text: An alias, chosen freely like `b`
choices.why: `b` is the alias. `Book` has to match an `@Entity` class, or Hibernate refuses the query.

prompt: Why does `BookService.list()` build the `BookResponse` records itself, instead of returning the `Book` entities to the controller?
hint: Where does the transaction end, and what still needs the database after that?

choices.text: Controllers are not allowed to import classes annotated with `@Entity`
choices.why: Nothing forbids it, and it would compile. The problem shows up when the code runs.

choices.text: Records are faster for Jackson to serialise than classes, and the list can be long
choices.why: Speed is not the reason. The reason is what the mapping reads: the author's name, from a lazy relationship.

choices.text: The author's name only loads while the service's transaction is open
choices.why: Right. Built inside the transaction, the records carry the names; an entity handed out would reach the controller detached, and the last section shows the exception that follows.

choices.text: The entity has no getters the controller could call
choices.why: It has getters for every field. They work on a detached book; it is the lazy author behind `getAuthor()` that cannot load.

prompt: With the `sql` profile on, `curl -s localhost:8080/books/2` runs `BookService.get`, which calls `em.find(Book.class, 2L)` and then `BookResponse.from`. How many SQL statements does the request send?
hint: `find` loads the book alone, and the author is lazy.

prompt: Inside one transaction, `em.find(Book.class, 3L)` is called twice. What happens?
hint: The persistence context is a map from key to object.

choices.text: One SELECT, and the same object returned both times
choices.why: Right: the log showed one `select` and `the same object twice: true`.

choices.text: Two SELECTs, and two different objects that are `equals` to each other
choices.why: That is what two JDBC queries do. Inside one persistence context, the second `find` is answered by the map.

choices.text: Two SELECTs, and the same object returned both times
choices.why: The same object, yes, but no second `select`: the map already holds book 3.

choices.text: One SELECT, and a copy of the first object the second time
choices.why: A copy would make `==` false. The demonstration printed `true`.

prompt: `RepriceOnce` changed a field and never called a save method. Why did an UPDATE reach the database?
hint: It came out after both log lines, not when `reprice` ran.

choices.text: `reprice` sends an UPDATE as soon as it changes the field
choices.why: Both log lines came out before the `update`; nothing is sent when the field changes. Hibernate does not even see that moment.

choices.text: Spring calls `save` on every entity at the end of a `@Transactional` method
choices.why: Spring only commits the transaction. What writes the change is Hibernate, during the flush that the commit starts.

choices.text: The commit compared the book with its copy from loading
choices.why: Right. That is dirty checking: the flush writes an `UPDATE` for every managed object whose values changed.

choices.text: PostgreSQL saw the new price in the open connection and stored it
choices.why: The database knows nothing about Java objects. It only stores what an SQL statement tells it to.

prompt: The bookshop is started a second time with `RepriceOnce` still in it. The book is loaded and `reprice(3800)` is called again, but the log shows no UPDATE. Why?
hint: What does the flush compare?

choices.text: The persistence context remembered the first run's UPDATE and skipped it
choices.why: A persistence context lives for one transaction, and this is a new process. Nothing from the first run is remembered.

choices.text: Hibernate only writes an entity once per application start
choices.why: There is no such rule; any transaction can write any entity. The second run had nothing to write.

choices.text: `@Order(1)` made it run after the commit of the catalogue report
choices.why: `@Order(1)` only puts this task before the report. Each runs its own transaction.

choices.text: The row already said 3800, so nothing differed
choices.why: Right. Dirty checking compares values, not calls: setting a field to what it already holds is no change.

prompt: Put what happens during `RepriceOnce.run` in order.
hint: Nothing is written until the method has returned.
items: The first find sends a SELECT and keeps a copy of the row's values
The second find returns the same object without any SQL
reprice changes the price on the object, and nothing is sent
The method returns, and the transaction begins to commit
The flush compares the object with its copy and sends an UPDATE
trap: The UPDATE does not follow the call to reprice; it follows the comparison at the commit.

prompt: The plain query loaded six books, but the log showed only four SELECTs on `author`. Why not six?
hint: Two authors wrote two books each.

choices.text: Hibernate batches the last two authors into one statement
choices.why: No batching is configured; each statement in the log names one id. The last two books sent nothing at all.

choices.text: Two books have no author
choices.why: `author_id` is `NOT NULL`, and every book in the JSON has an author's name.

choices.text: The second book by an author found that author already in the persistence context
choices.why: Right. Machado de Assis and H. G. Wells were loaded for their first books; Quincas Borba and The War of the Worlds were answered by the map.

choices.text: PostgreSQL answered the repeated statements from its cache without Hibernate sending them
choices.why: A statement the database answers from a cache is still a statement in Hibernate's log. These were never sent.

prompt: A page lists 20 books written by 3 different authors, using `select b from Book b` with a LAZY author, and reads every author's name inside one transaction. How many SQL statements does it send?
hint: One for the list, then one per author that is not yet in the persistence context.

prompt: After `LAZY` was changed to `EAGER`, the list still sent one SELECT on `book` and four on `author`. Why did EAGER not help?
hint: Who wrote the SQL for the list, and did it mention the author?

choices.text: The query names no author, so they still load one by one
choices.why: Right. `EAGER` decides that the author arrives with the book, not how; a JPQL query is translated as written. It only helped `find`, whose SQL Hibernate writes itself.

choices.text: EAGER takes effect only after the application is restarted twice
choices.why: The application was rebuilt and restarted once, and the change did take effect: the authors were loaded at query time instead of later.

choices.text: EAGER applies to `@OneToMany` only
choices.why: It applies to `@ManyToOne` too, and `find` on one book became a single joined `select`.

choices.text: The persistence context ignores EAGER inside a read-only transaction
choices.why: `readOnly` skips change detection. It does not change how relationships load.

prompt: `LazyInitializationException: Could not initialize proxy [com.example.bookshop.catalogue.Author#1] - no session`. What does it say?
hint: Session is Hibernate's word for the persistence context.

choices.text: Author 1 does not exist in the database
choices.why: Then there would be no proxy: book 1 points at author 1 and the row is there. The proxy could not ask for it.

choices.text: The HTTP session that Tomcat keeps for the user who sent the request had expired
choices.why: The bookshop has no HTTP sessions. Here session means Hibernate's session, the persistence context.

choices.text: The connection pool ran out of connections
choices.why: Then the error would come from the pool, waiting for a connection. Here nobody even tried to get one.

choices.text: The author was read after its book's persistence context closed
choices.why: Right. Without a transaction around `get`, the book was detached by the time `BookResponse.from` asked for the name.

prompt: With `@Transactional` removed from `get`, the request failed with `open-in-view=false` and worked with `open-in-view=true`. What did the setting change?
hint: When does each setting open and close the persistence context?

choices.text: It made `get` transactional again
choices.why: No transaction was involved: the author was loaded by a persistence context with none, kept open by the setting.

choices.text: It kept a persistence context open for the whole web request, so the proxy could still load
choices.why: Right. Open session in view opens one when the request arrives and closes it after the response, and the author's `select` ran inside it.

choices.text: It loaded every author into memory at start-up, before the first request arrived, so no query was needed
choices.why: The log of that request showed the author's `select` running during the request, after the book's.

choices.text: It switched the relationship to EAGER for web requests
choices.why: The book was still loaded alone and the author by a second statement, which is lazy loading.

prompt: Why is `spring.jpa.open-in-view` set to `false` in the bookshop? Choose all that apply.
hint: The section gives three reasons.

choices.text: Any code touching a getter can run a query, so the service no longer decides what is loaded
choices.why: Right. With it off, the service's transaction is the only place loading happens.

choices.text: It can hold a database connection until the response has been written
choices.why: Right, including the time a slow client takes to receive it; lesson 14 counts connections.

choices.text: It only exists for web requests, so the same code can work from a controller and fail from a start-up task
choices.why: Right. A scheduled job or a `CommandLineRunner` gets no such context.

choices.text: With it on, Hibernate refuses `join fetch` queries
choices.why: A `join fetch` query can run either way. OSIV changes how long the persistence context lives, not what queries may say.

choices.text: With it on, dirty checking stops working
choices.why: Dirty checking happens at a commit, and OSIV changes nothing there.

prompt: A colleague's version of the bookshop has a `@Transactional` service that returns `List<Book>` entities, and a controller that maps them with `BookResponse.from`. `findAll` has no `join fetch` and `open-in-view` is false. What does `GET /books` do?
hint: Where does the transaction end, and where is the author's name read?

choices.text: It works, sending one SELECT on book and then one on author for each of the four authors, as the lesson counted
choices.why: Those statements would need an open persistence context, and the mapping runs in the controller, after the service's transaction has closed.

choices.text: It fails with a LazyInitializationException when the controller reads the first author's name
choices.why: Right. The entities leave the transaction detached and their authors are still proxies, so the first `getName()` in the controller throws.

choices.text: It works, with a single joined SELECT
choices.why: Nothing asked for a join: without `join fetch` the query loads books alone.

choices.text: It fails at start-up, when the catalogue report asks for the list before any request has arrived
choices.why: The catalogue report calls `list().size()`, which counts entities without touching an author. Start-up succeeds; the request fails.

prompt: Inside a `@Transactional` method, a book is loaded with `find`, its title is changed on the object, and then a later line throws a `RuntimeException`, so the transaction rolls back. Is the new title in the database afterwards?
hint: When does dirty checking send its UPDATE, and what does a rollback do with it?

choices.text: Yes: changing a managed object writes it straight away
choices.why: The reprice demonstration showed the opposite: both log lines came out before any `update`. The change waits for the flush.

choices.text: Yes, because dirty checking runs even when the method throws
choices.why: A flush on the way to a rollback would only send statements the rollback then undoes. Nothing the transaction did is kept.

choices.text: No, because `find` returns a copy that is never written back
choices.why: `find` returns a managed object, the one the persistence context watches. A commit would have written it.

choices.text: No: there was no commit to write it
choices.why: Right. The object changed in memory only; lesson 14 shows rollback on the bookshop's own orders.

prompt: With the lesson's final code, put the steps of `GET /books` in order.
hint: The transaction is the service's, and the JSON is written last.
items: One SELECT joins book and author
Each Book is mapped to a BookResponse, with its author's name already loaded
The transaction commits and the persistence context closes
Jackson writes the records as JSON
trap: The records are built before the commit; that is what lets the persistence context close without anything left to load.

prompt: Starting from the lesson's final code, which of these changes would bring the N+1 statements back to `GET /books`? Choose all that apply.
hint: N+1 needs two things: a query that leaves the authors out, and code that reads them.

choices.text: Removing `join fetch b.author` from the query
choices.why: Right. That is exactly the version the lesson counted: one SELECT on book and four on author.

choices.text: Removing `join fetch b.author` and changing the relationship to EAGER
choices.why: Right. The EAGER detour showed the same five statements, sent at query time instead of later.

choices.text: Setting `spring.jpa.open-in-view=true`
choices.why: The query still joins the authors, so nothing is left to load lazily, whoever keeps the context open.

choices.text: Removing `@Transactional(readOnly = true)` from `list()`
choices.why: The authors arrive with the books in the joined query, so the mapping touches no proxy, and the query runs the same with or without the annotation.

prompt: Match each symptom to its cause.
hint: Each symptom appeared in this lesson.

pairs.right: a lazy field read after the transaction ended

pairs.left: a column of identical SELECTs on author in the log
pairs.right: a lazy relationship read in a loop

pairs.left: an UPDATE that no code in the project contains
pairs.right: a managed object changed before the commit

pairs.left: column "author_id" of relation "book" does not exist
pairs.right: a table left over from an older schema

right_distractors: a JPQL query that names a table instead of an entity
